rows.title: Introduction to Financial Accounting
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Students will demonstrate the ability to define and complete the steps in the accounting cycle including journalizing and posting financial transactions, recording adjusting and closing entries, and preparation of financial reports.
Students will demonstrate the ability to identify and record changes in assets, liabilities and owner's equity through the recording and posting of journal entries.

Students will demonstrate the ability to prepare and explain the purpose, structure, content, and underlying principles of the general-purpose financial statements including the income statement, balance sheet, statement of changes in stockholders' equity, and statement of cash flows.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Explain the nature and purpose of generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) and International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS).
Explain the role of accounting in organizations and organizational decision-making.

Explain and apply the components of the conceptual framework for financial accounting and reporting, including the qualitative characteristics of accounting information, the assumptions underlying accounting, the basic principles of financial accounting, and the constraints and limitations on accounting information.
Define and use accounting and business terminology.
Explain what a system is and how an accounting system is designed to satisfy the needs of specific businesses and users.
Summarize the purpose of journals and ledgers.
Apply transaction analysis, input transactions into the accounting system, process this input, and prepare and interpret the four basic financial statements.

Discuss the purpose, structure, content, and underlying principles of the general-purpose financial statements including the income statement, balance sheet, statement of changes in shareholders' equity, and statement of cash flows.

Explain the content, form, and purpose of the basic financial statements (including footnotes) and the annual report, and how they satisfy the information needs of investors, creditors, and other users.
Illustrate and apply accounting policy choices in the preparation and analysis of financial statements, inclucing, but not limited to: inventory cost flow assumptions and depreciation methods.
Distinguish between cash basis and accrual basis accounting and their impact on the financial statements, including the revenue recognition and matching principles.
Identify and illustrate how the principles of internal control are used to manage and control the firm's resources and minimize risk.
Explain the nature of current assets and related issues, including the measurement and reporting of cash and cash equivalents, receivables and bad debts, and inventory and cost of goods sold.
Identify and illustrate issues relating to long-term asset acquisition, use, cost allocation, and disposal.
Distinguish between capital and revenue expenditures.
Explain the valuation and reporting of current liabilities, estimated liabilities, and other contingencies.
Identify and illustrate issues relating to long-term liabilities, including issuance, valuation, and retirement of debt (including the time value of money).
Identify and illustrate issues relating to stockholders' equity, including issuance, repurchase of capital stock, and dividends.
Explain the importance of operating, investing, and financing activities reported in the Statement of Cash Flows.
Interpret company activity, profitability, liquidity, and solvency through selection and application of appropriate financial analysis tools.
Identify the ethical implications inherent in financial reporting and be able to apply strategies for addressing them.

rows.title: Nursing Pharmacology
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Describe basic pharmacological concepts including pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics and be able to appropriately apply the professional language associated with pharmacology.

Describe the specific pharmacology of common drug classes by body system used in allied health and nursing including their mechanisms of action, indications, uses, contraindications, interactions with medications, foods and herbs, and major adverse effects.
Examine relevant government legislation related to inventory of medication and the role of the health professional in safe and effective administration of selected medications.
Accurately calculate doses for common medications.
Use technology correctly to obtain accurate pharmacology as it applies to patient care.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Explain the history and evolution of pharmacology.
Determine the four sources of drugs and the classification system of medications.
Differentiate key terms and abbreviations used in pharmacology and medication administration.
Discuss the drug cycle and their effects on the body.
Differentiate between therapeutic level and potency of a drug.
Compare and contrast drug interactions, side effects, and adverse reactions.
Identify reliable resources for drug information, both written and electronic.
Describe considerations in patient safety in drug administration.
List the seven rights of medication administration.
Describe how age, weight, route of administration, dose, other medications, elimination, distribution, underlying disease and other variables affect medication administration.
Discuss cultural implications of medication use and administration.
Identify actions taken during accidental or deliberate overdose of medications.
Identify the roles of the Federal Drug Administration (FDA) and the Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) in patient safety.
Compare and contrast chemical, generic, brand and trade names of drugs.
Discuss how drugs are developed.
Discuss illegal street drugs and slang terminology.
Identify controlled substances, the classification system, and purpose.
Describe substance abuse, addiction, and tolerance to drugs.
Discuss the role of health care professionals in identifying and reporting impaired patients and healthcare workers.
Identify the components of a legal prescription and a medication order and who can prescribe.
Interpret labels safely.
Discuss written labels from manufacturers and pharmacies, and e-prescriptions.
Accurately problem solve using fractions, decimals, ratios and proportions, and conversions.
Perform accurate computations using fundamental math concepts.
Compare and contrast the four measurement systems.
Explain the fundamental units of the metric, apothecary, household and Fahrenheit/Celsius systems of measurement.
Perform calculations within and between the systems of measurement.
Perform calculations with the four methods of dosage calculation: ratio and proportion, dimensional analysis, the fraction method, and the formulation method.
Explain how to reconstitute powdered medication.
Discuss the use of regulator pumps for intravenous medications.
Discuss the basics of intravenous therapy.
Accurately calculate fluid balance.
Identify and explain the routes of drug administration, including identifying and locating various injection sites.
Describe the possible enteral routes for administering medications.
Explain how to administer enteral medications including nasogastric and gastric tubes.
Identify safety measures related to enteral medication administration and the correlation to potential side effects and adverse effects to medications/ enteral therapy.
Describe the possible parenteral routes for administering medications.
Explain how to administer parenteral medications including topical, ophthalmic, optic, nasal, inhalation, vaginal, and injectable medications.
Identify safety measures related to parenteral medication administration and the correlation to potential side effects and adverse effects to medications/ parenteral therapy.
Describe the anatomy and physiology of the Integumentary System, common disorders, common medications, and lifespan considerations.
Describe the anatomy and physiology of the Musculoskeletal System, common disorders, common medications, and lifespan considerations.
Describe the anatomy and physiology of the Nervous System, common disorders, common medications, and lifespan considerations.
Describe the anatomy and physiology of the Endocrine System, common disorders, common medications, and lifespan considerations.
Describe the anatomy and physiology of the Cardiovascular System, common disorders, common medications, and lifespan considerations.
Describe the anatomy and physiology of the Immune/Lymphatic System, common disorders, common medications, and lifespan considerations.
Describe the anatomy and physiology of the Pulmonary System, common disorders, common medications, and lifespan considerations.
Describe the anatomy and physiology of the Gastrointestinal System, common disorders, common medications, and lifespan considerations.
Describe the anatomy and physiology of the Reproductive and Urinary Systems, common disorders, common medications, and lifespan considerations.
Discuss the body’s need for vitamins and minerals.
Compare and contrast Eastern and Western Medicine.
Discuss herbal therapies and why patients may prefer to prescribed medications.
Explain complementary and alternative medicine and why insurance companies do not usually pay for these treatments.

rows.title: Human Anatomy and Physiology I
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify the various parts and functionality of the light microscope.
Understand the different structures and functions of a human cell.
Identify the different histological types of tissues.
Recognize gross anatomy of the Integumentary, Skeletal, Muscular, and/or Nervous systems.
Explain physiological processes of the Integumentary, Skeletal, Muscular, and/or Nervous systems.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Define anatomy and physiology; list and describe the major characteristics of life; list and describe the requirements of living organisms.
Explain the importance of homeostasis for survival.
List the major cavities and major organ systems and their organs; be able to use the descriptive terminology of anatomy and physiology.
Discuss and explain how the study of living material is dependent on the study of biochemistry: its atoms, molecules, compounds, chemical reactions, and its ability to regulate acid-base balance.
Describe and list the major organic and inorganic substances within the body and explain how they aid the chemistry of the cell.

Explain the general characteristics of the cell; how the cell's structure is related to its functions; each organelle and its functions within the cell; how substances move into and out of the cell; the life cycle of the cell; and its reproductive cycles including how the cellular reproduction is controlled.
Discuss anabolism versus catabolism; enzymes control metabolic processes; cellular respiration; how energy is made available for cellular activity; and the pathways for metabolic regulation.
Describe how genetic information is stored in the DNA molecule and explain how DNA and RNA are used in the processes of protein synthesis.
Explain how and why DNA is replicated and describe how genetic information can be altered.
List and identify the four basic tissue types and identify the specific cellular types within each tissue.
Describe how each tissue helps to maintain homeostasis of life processes.
Identify and describe the four major types of membranes.
Describe the characteristics of various layers of skin and their functions.
Describe the accessory organs of the skin and their functions.
List and describe the components of skin color and the genetic traits.
Define osteology and classify bones according to their shapes and give an example of each.
Describe the general structure of bone and list the functions of its part.
Explain how bone develops; distinguish between the axial and appendicular skeletons and name and number the bones of each.
Explain and describe the structures and functions of the articulating joints.
Explain how joints can be classified by the type of tissue that binds the bones together.
List the six types of synovial joints and give an example of each.
Explain how skeletal muscles produce movement at joints and identify several types of movement.
Define myology and describe the macro and microscopic structure of muscle tissue.
Explain the major events that occur during muscle contraction.
Explain muscle cell metabolism during rest and during contraction.
Distinguish between fast and slow muscle, explain and compare the structure and functions of the three types of muscle tissues.
Describe the locations of the major skeletal muscles of each body region and describe the action of each muscle group.
List and identify the structure and functions of the spinal cord, brain.
Discuss the function of peripheral nervous system.
Explain the importance and the function(s) of the autonomic nervous system.
Distinguish among motor, sensory, and association areas of the cerebral cortex.
Explain what is meant by hemisphere dominance.
List the cranial and spinal nerves and their functions.
Use lab models, charts, A&P handouts, and the binocular compound light microscope to study and identify cells, tissues, and organs of the body systems studied during the semester.
Demonstrate safe and effective use of all laboratory equipment.

rows.title: Introduction to Archaeology
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Demonstrate an understanding of the scientific method and its application to archaeological research.
Describe the archaeological methods and theory used to analyze and interpret the human past.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Discuss the scientific method, including its steps and utility in conducting archaeological research.
Describe the theoretical and historical relationship between archaeology and anthropology.
Describe the theoretical frameworks, methodologies, and field techniques used to interpret the archaeological record.
Identify the methods of archaeological analysis and classification typology with reference to cultural sequence.
Describe the goals and legal and ethical considerations of cultural resource management and working with descendent communities.

rows.title: Cultural Anthropology - Honors
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Evaluate the conceptual frameworks that drive the practice of cultural anthropology in relation to the promotion of social justice.
Apply a relativist attitude in analyzing a social problem from various cultural perspectives.

Honors: Apply an anthropological, theoretical approach to the evaluation of a specific case study related to product design, social justice, or cultural appropriation through completing the Honors project research and presentation.
objectives: Explain the role of cultural anthropology within the broader discipline of anthropology.
Analyze and reflect on the anthropological concept of culture in relation to key theoretical perspectives.
Demonstrate an understanding of anthropological concepts including ethnicity, gender, political organization, economic systems, kinship, rituals, and belief systems.
Apply and appraise a relativist view to the study of cultural difference.
Explain the main method of studying culture and interpret ethical implications of practicing such.
Evaluate the relation between globalization and culture.
Honors: Evaluate anthropological approaches and interpret research presented in an ethnographic text.
Honors: Formulate a research project that applies anthropological perspectives to the study of a contemporary human problem.

rows.title: Magic, Witchcraft, and Religion
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Evaluate a variety of religious beliefs and practices across cultures.
Apply anthropological research methods and theoretical approaches to the analysis of religion, magic and witchcraft and their respective practices.
Analyze the interaction of belief systems and religious traditions, including magic and witchcraft with the physical and social environment.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Introduce the relationship between magic and witchcraft within religious belief systems and anthropological theory.
Provide a historical overview from past to present of the development of beliefs and practices associated with magic, witchcraft, and religion.
Examine the central myths, ideas and worldview of various cultural groups across the world.
Differentiate between the various roles of traditional religious specialists and how these operate within social systems.
Introduce primary sources relevant to the study of magic, witchcraft, and religion.

rows.title: Introduction to Biological Anthropology
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Demonstrate understanding of the scientific method, genetics, and evolutionary processes to interpret human origins, adaptation, and variation.
Examine and compare primate and hominin anatomical, behavioral, fossil, and genetic evidence to evaluate evolutionary relationships and trends.
Investigate modern human diversity, explaining the interaction of biology and culture in shaping variation while recognizing the invalidity of race as a biological concept.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Demonstrate an understanding of the scientific method and an ability to interpret data to arrive at reasoned conclusions.
Identify the principles of human inheritance, molecular biology, genetics, and evolutionary processes from the perspective of biological anthropology.
Identify the biological and cultural factors responsible for human variation.
Identify and compare primate and hominin species in terms of their osteological, morphological, and/or behavioral adaptations.

rows.title: Biological Anthropology Lab
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Demonstrate understanding of the scientific method, genetics, and evolutionary processes to interpret human origins, adaptation, and variation.
Examine and compare primate and hominin anatomical, behavioral, fossil, and genetic evidence to evaluate evolutionary relationships and trends.
Investigate modern human diversity, explaining the interaction of biology and culture in shaping variation while recognizing the invalidity of race as a biological concept.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Demonstrate an understanding of the scientific method and an ability to interpret data to arrive at reasoned conclusions.
Describe the principles of human inheritance, genetics, and evolutionary processes.
Identify and compare primate and hominin species in terms of their osteological,morphological, and/or behavioral adaptations.

rows.title: Art Appreciation
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
To introduce students to various artworks, both historical and contemporary.
To establish an understanding of cultural, social,political, personal and universal, connections.
Develop language associated with artistic practices, critique, analysis and evaluation of artwork and architecture.
Develop observational skills to better understand the world in which they inhabit.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Define key vocabulary and terms used within field of the visual arts.
Discuss the different methods of producing art throughout particular time periods, evaluate and critique unique characteristics of each.
Analyze, evaluate and critique works of art and architecture based on the elements and principles of design.
Discuss the historical and contemporary significance of major artistic movements.
Discuss the importance of the arts in understanding various cultures, and the meaning of their particular artistic sensibilities through a broad and inclusive lens.
Discuss the role of art, and the artist in society, and the value and purpose of the arts within various cultures and time periods, and the interconnected purpose of creating art throughout history.

rows.title: Survey of Asian Art
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify specific terms and vocabulary related to the different styles and methods in art and architectural production as related to Asian countries.
Identify specific art and architectural works from different periods and locations in Asia.
Identify Asian art as related to the sociopolitical, cultural and historic context.
Critique, interpret and identify the Asian art as related to wider global context.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Discuss, compare and contrast representative works of art from India, Southeast Asia, China, Japan, and Korea using learned basic visual arts vocabulary.

Analyze, discuss and differentiate representative artworks and architecture in terms of cultural values, diverse religions, and socio-political circumstances and compare, contrast, and critique artwork in a historical as well as cultural context.
Analyze, discuss, interpret, and differentiate the role of Asian art, architecture, and artists of prehistoric to the contemporary times.
Differentiate and understand the contributions of distinct Asian cultures to Western art and architecture.

rows.title: Foundations of Three-Dimensional Design
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Ability to recognize and discuss the Principles and Elements of Three-Dimensional Design.
Apply principles and elements of Three-Dimensional Design into original work of design.
Evaluate, analyze, discuss, and critique their own design work and the work of others.
Learn to use research as an investigative tool, and make connections to contemporary issues in art and design.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Demonstrate an understanding of the terminology and fundamental principles of three-dimensional design.
Respond creatively to material and space.
Successfully create three dimensional forms using the knowledge and techniques learned in the course.
Demonstrate knowledge in the use of materials, tools and techniques, along with their application in design.
Demonstrate knowledge of various historical and contemporary three dimensional design approaches, with an emphasis on aesthetics and culture.

rows.title: Drawing II
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Further develop basic skills to advance their drawings and artworks towards a personal artistic, creative and meaningful expression.
Develop research skills for a refined understanding of contemporary and historical drawings, processes, and media.
Support their personal search for content and meaning as evidenced within the artwork.
Understand the need for excellence within the craft and skill set that comprise and build their portfolios for transfer and employment opportunities.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Produce drawings that creatively apply and interpret two-dimensional design elements and principles, including understanding color as an additional means of visual communication
Critically evaluate and analyze processes, concepts and aesthetics of artworks, and apply critical thought to their own works and that of others.
Create a portfolio of artwork in various mediums and genres that support their learned skills, dedication, and personal creative voice.

rows.title: Life Drawing I
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Demonstrate fundamental skills associated with figure drawing to render the human form on a two-dimensional surface. 2. Identify significant structures of the skeletal and muscular systems and demonstrate an understanding of these structure through their drawings. 3. Scale the human figure to the page from observation in a variety of vantage points. 4. Discuss, analyze, evaluate and critique their own drawings and the drawings of others.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Make informed choices regarding traditional and contemporary approaches, media, and their applications.
Demonstrate the fundamental skills associated with figure drawing to render the human form on a two-dimensional surface.
Identify significant structures of the skeletal and muscular systems and demonstrate an understanding of these structure through their drawings.
Scale the human figure to the page from observation in a variety of vantage points.
Make visual and conceptual connections between the fundamental techniques of figure drawing and the contemporary art world.
Discuss, analyze, evaluate and critique their own drawings and the drawings of others.

rows.title: Painting II
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Continued study of painting with a focus on development of learned skills, and sustained engagement in painting as an artistic practice.
Develop artistic problem solving skills as related to complex formal and conceptual difficulties.
Foster mature, relevant research skills related to contemporary painting practices, which will inform the development of the artwork.
Enhance portfolio development with work that addresses varied artistic, personal, cultural, social, global concerns, as determined by student interest and skills.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Create paintings that address more complex, thoughtful personal, universal, artistic concerns.
Make informed choices regarding both traditional, alternative and experimental painting media and surfaces and their applications.
Discuss, and understand traditional, alternative, and experimental painting media, including qualities and applications.
Critically discuss trends, processes, concepts and aesthetics within the field of painting, and formal concerns within their own body of work.
Discuss, analyze, evaluate and critique their own painting and the paintings of others.
Prepare and present a portfolio of work in varied mediums, artistic processes that demonstrates intermediate painting techniques and directions, both formally and conceptually.

rows.title: Survey of Art from Prehistory to the Medieval Era
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: When shown an image of a major work of art, the student will correctly identify the name, country or place of origin and date.
When asked to analyze the difference between two major works or aft, the student will effectively compare and contrast styles and themes portrayed.
objectives: Part 1 - Common Course Objectives:
Identify, examine, and assess representative works of art and architecture from prehistory to the medieval era employing appropriate art historical terminology.
Analyze works of art and architecture in terms of aesthetic, socio-political, religious,historical, technological, and cultural contexts in which they were created
Develop critical thinking, information literacy, and problem solving through an engagement with art, architecture, artists, and patrons from prehistory to the medieval era.
Part 2 - Local Course Objectives:
Identify major works of art and architecture from ancient times to the Middle Ages.
Compare and contrast the styles and themes portrayed in a variety of works of art and architecture.
Evaluate and critique works of art based on historical context, subject matter, theme, form, composition, material, technique, line, color, space, mass, volume, perspective, proportion, and scale.
Recognize patterns and themes presented in the history of art and architecture.
Analyze images of art and architecture from a historical as well as aesthetic perspective.

rows.title: Survey of Art from the Renaissance to Contemporary
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Demonstrate the ability to compare and contrast different artworks and modes of expression from different time periods and geographic locations with the use of design elements and principles.
Distinguish different Periods, Locations and Individual Styles in its historic context, via primary and secondary resources.
Demonstrate the ethical use of sources and provide properly formatted citations in formal papers.

Demonstrate in the written reports, essays and orally the understanding of the similarities and differences of diverse human experience via analysis of artifacts from Renaissance to Contemporary times (Western focus)
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Common Course Objective
Identify, examine, and assess representative works of art and architecture from the Renaissance to the contemporary period employing appropriate art historical terminology.
Analyze works of art and architecture and critique them in terms of aesthetic, sociopolitical, religious, historical, technological, and cultural contexts in which they were created.
Develop critical thinking, information literacy, and problem solving through an engagement with art, architecture, artists, and patrons from the Renaissance to the contemporary period.
Additional Course Objectives
Articulate an understanding of and demonstrate an appreciation of the value and importance of art museums, galleries and other cultural institutions within their communities.

rows.title: American Sign Language I
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Expressive Communication: Students will demonstrate signed ASL proficiency with proper production and clarity, speed and fluency, non-manual markers, and grammatical concepts, with an accuracy level of 70%+ (for a “3” score) or 85%+ (for a “4” score). Topics will include vocabulary covered in Signing Naturally units 1-5.

Receptive Communication and Linguistics: Students will interpret ASL segments containing vocabulary from units 1-5 with an accuracy level of 70%+ (for a “3” score) or 85%+ (for a “4” score) and demonstrate understanding of ASL grammar structures and concepts.

Cultural Diversity and Appreciation: Students will demonstrate appropriate knowledge of the Deaf Community regarding social interactions, beliefs, values, arts, literature, entertainment, diversity, and current events, at a superficial level. They will interact with, members of the Deaf Community, compare and contrast cultural norms, and appreciate the similarities and differences within the Deaf community and in comparison, with their own. Upon completion, students will reflect on their language use, strengths, areas for improvement, and outline a specific plan for continual language growth.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Introduce self and interact in Deaf culturally appropriate ways including getting a Deaf person’s attention, asking for repetition, and using a culturally appropriate style of communication

Engage in conversations about a variety of basic topics including introductions, personal information, academics, family and relationships, residences and communities, daily/weekly/monthly schedules, and leisure activities.

Use basic ASL grammar structure, including y/n-questions, wh-questions, rhetorical questions, topic/comment sentence structure, directional verbs, real world orientation and spatial agreement, contrastive structure, and simple classifiers.
Incorporate appropriate facial expressions and non-manual signals, pronouns, fingerspelling, loan signs, and cardinal and ordinal number structures into basic conversations.
Compare and contrast communication modes used by Deaf persons and the advantages and disadvantages of these modes.
Discuss in an informed manner the social, medical, and educational issues faced by Deaf persons in the United States.

rows.title: American Sign Language II
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Expressive Communication: Students will demonstrate signed ASL proficiency with proper production and clarity, speed and fluency, non-manual markers, and grammatical concepts, with an accuracy level of 70%+ (for a “3” score) or 85%+ (for a “4” score). Topics will include vocabulary covered in Signing Naturally units 7-11.

Receptive Communication and Linguistics: Students will interpret ASL segments containing vocabulary from Signing Naturally units 7-11 with an accuracy level of 70%+ (for a “3” score) or 85%+ (for a “4” score) and demonstrate understanding of ASL grammar structures and concepts.

Cultural Diversity and Appreciation: Students will demonstrate appropriate knowledge of the Deaf Community regarding social interactions, beliefs, values, arts, literature, entertainment, diversity, and current events, at a intermediate level. They will interact with members of the Deaf Community, compare and contrast cultural norms, and appreciate the similarities and differences within the Deaf community and in comparison, with their own. Upon completion, students will reflect on their language use, strengths, areas for improvement, and outline a specific plan for continual language growth. They will compare and contrast cultural norms between Hearing, Deaf, and deaf cultures (yes, Deaf and deaf are two different groups), and explain the values held by each group in terms of hearing status, language use, social circles, and political perspectives on deafness.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Introduce self and interact in Deaf culturally appropriate ways including getting a Deaf person’s attention, interrupting a conversation, opening and closing a conversation, providing feedback, and using a culturally appropriate style of communication
Engage in conversations about a variety of basic topics including food, personal appearances, housing and floor plans, finances and the workplace, wellness and fitness, and destinations

Use basic ASL grammar structure, including y/n-questions, wh-questions, rhetorical questions, topic/comment sentence structure, directional verbs, real world orientation and spatial agreement, contrastive structure, and simple classifiers

Incorporate appropriate facial expressions and non-manual signals, pronouns, fluent fingerspelling, loan signs, roleshifting, and various number structures such as cardinal/ordinal number, clock numbers, and money signs into conversations
Compare and contrast communication modes used by Deaf persons and the advantages and disadvantages of these modes
Discuss in an informed manner the social, medical, and educational issues faced by Deaf persons in the United States
Demonstrate an understanding of the differences between hearing and Deaf cultures, in regards to language, norms, and mores

rows.title: American Sign Language III
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Interpret visual/signed ASL at an intermediate level
Demonstrate language proficiency by signing American Sign Language at an intermediate level

Demonstrate advanced knowledge of the Deaf community regarding social interactions, beliefs, values, arts, literature, entertainment, and diversity/multiculturalism (various identities and intersectionality with different languages used in USA)
Define the concept of culture, appreciate other cultures and interact with members of those cultures in relation to their own
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Communicate comfortably, appropriately and effectively in conversations discussing language conventions, narratives, storytelling, history, and classifiers of various sorts.

Demonstrate comprehension and production of ASL grammatical strategies such as; role shifting, time indicators to specify tense, non-manual markers to indicate distance and location of items, use of both hands to indicate relation of items, inflection for temporal aspects such as recurring and continual, spatial agreement, plain verbs, transitions, narrative structures, sequencing orders, use of continuity, and descriptive and instrumental classifiers.

Compose and demonstrate ASL dialogues and/or narratives with ASL linguistic functions expressing a complaint, making a suggestion and requests, describes a life event, describes a weekend activity, tell a family immigration history, and describing items of various types and from various perspectives.

Apply sensitivity to Deaf culture in staged role-play interactions in terms of regulating the pace of a conversation in ASL, opening and resuming a conversation, and directing and maintaining attention.
Identify the differences in conversational patterns and linguistics of the Deaf and hearing communities.
Identify contemporary issues facing diverse members of the Deaf community within the United States.

Demonstrate a continued sensitivity of the Deaf and the needs within the community through attendance of Deaf events, and involvement in schools, institutions and organizations serving the Deaf persons.

rows.title: American Sign Language IV
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
interpret visual/signed ASL at a beginning to intermediate level
demonstrate language proficiency by signing American Sign Language at a beginning to intermediate level

demonstrate appropriate knowledge of the Deaf community regarding social interactions, beliefs, values, arts, literature, entertainment, and diversity/multiculturalism (various identities and intersectionality with different languages used in USA)
define the concept of culture, appreciate other cultures and interact with members of those cultures in relation to their own.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Engage in conversations about a variety of topics including health and the human body, sports, science, unforgettable moments, interesting facts, and everyday rules.
Identify and apply advanced rules of ASL including role shifting sequencing, listing skills, spatial agreement, making comparisons, action sequencing, and classifier use.

Incorporate appropriate facial expressions and non-manual signals, pronouns, fluent finger spelling, loan signs, role-shifting, and various number structures such as fractions, percentages, ratios, money signs, and other statistics into conversations.
Use American Sign Language confidently in a variety of formal and informal contexts, including presentations and storytelling.
Analyze contemporary issues facing the Deaf community in the United States.
Recognize and discuss the contributions of Deaf people from diverse backgrounds throughout history.
Demonstrate a deeper sensitivity of the Deaf community and the need for professionals in the field through continued involvement in events through Deaf schools, institutions and other organizations.
Demonstrate deeper understanding of the impacts of Audism, Ableism & Linguicism.

rows.title: The American Deaf Experience: Introduction to Deaf Studies
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Culture: Students will define the concept of culture and demonstrate appropriate knowledge of the Deaf community regarding social interactions, beliefs, values, arts, literature, entertainment, and diversity. Students will also interact with members of the culture.
History: Students will demonstrate knowledge of historical events throughout Deaf History from 1800’s-present day.
Politics and Social Movements: Students will demonstrate understanding of political views and social movements surrounding deafness and Deaf Culture
Famous People: Students will demonstrate understanding of famous Deaf people throughout history and their contributions to both Deaf and hearing cultures.
Contemporary Issues: Students will demonstrate awareness of contemporary issues that are occurring within the Deaf Community, including marginalized members and different language usage today.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

identify and appreciate the contributions of Deaf artists, writers and storytellers

rows.title: Fingerspelling, Numbers, Classifiers, and Non-Manuals
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Receptive: Identify complex finger spelled words at normal conversational speed through configuration, content, and context; accurately recognize numbers embedded in a variety of conversational topics; and analyze the semantic intent of a classifier in context and interpret its meaning.

Expressive: Demonstrate fluid expressive fingerspelling (including prefixes, suffixes, abbreviations, loan signs, double letters), construct numbers clearly and appropriately based on context, incorporate classifiers in standard conversation and stories, and effectively demonstrate various non-manual signals within conversations and stories.
Written: Discuss various aspects of ASL grammar, and analyze semantics, pragmatics, and registers of ASL based on mouth morphemes, facial expressions, body positioning, and other non-manual signals.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify complex fingerspelled words at normal conversational speed through configuration, content, and context.
Demonstrate fluid expressive fingerspelling including prefixes, suffixes, abbreviations, loan signs, double letters.
Accurately recognize numbers embedded in a variety of conversational topics.
Construct numbers clearly and appropriately based on context.
Analyze the semantic intent of a classifier in context and interpret its meaning.
Incorporate classifiers in standard conversation and stories.
Analyze semantics, pragmatics, and registers of ASL based on mouth morphemes, facial expressions, body positioning, and other non-manual signals.
Effectively demonstrate various non-manual signals within conversations and stories.
Discuss various aspects of ASL grammar and be able to apply them in casual conversation.

outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to: • Explain the human factors that may impact the global environment. • Describe the changing climate and the effects that this will play a role on earth. • Discuss the sustainability of this planet and changes that needs to be taken into consideration for the future.

Describe the major categories of pollution and approaches to pollution control
Define energy efficiency and net energy.
Explain how the trophic structure of natural ecosystems demonstrates the second law of thermodynamics.

Describe how risk assessment is used to evaluate pollution¿s hazards to human health.

Explain the relationship between population growth and economic development.

Student will distinguish between the income effect and the substitution effect of a given price change in a market for a specific commodity.

Distinguish between economic concepts of total, average and marginal valuations, in evaluating and optimizing the operation of a business, given specific information on the cost structure and revenue generation for a given market environment. The student will draw average and marginal cost and revenue schedules to summarize the profit-maximizing level of output for a competitive firm, given tabular data that summarizes the business environment. In addition, describe how the market structure changes in the case of a monopolistically competitive firm.

objectives: Part 1 - Common Course Numbering Objectives:

rows.title: Principles of Macroeconomics - Honors
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Critically evaluate current macroeconomic policy measures related to macro-economic policy. They will be able to pick a current newspaper article on federal tax or government spending policy and trace through the implications of the policy in terms of the predicted impacts on Gross Domestic Product, the federal budget, national employment, and overall inflation (using standard tools of aggregate and aggregate supply analysis). This analysis would be in the form of a brief review of the article, citing the items above.

Find recent moves by the U.S. Federal Reserve Bank, Open Market Committee, and state whether those actions are designed to change the money supply. Students will write a brief summary to analyze the monetary authority’s recent actions in terms of the intended impact on overall interest rates, national output, employment, and price stability.

Honors: Utilize economic theory to model an economic or social problem, develop interesting hypotheses, and examine the empirical validity of the model and hypotheses using suitable data and economic modeling methods. The model may pertain to contemporary economic issues or to issues in economic history or the history of economic thought. The model itself need not be original; the innovative contribution may instead lie in examining it with new bodies of data, or demonstrating the model with new media. This product will be formatted and presented to the class as the semester class project. Also a properly cited research paper will be delivered utilizing 6 authoritative resources.
objectives: Part 1 - Common Course Numbering Objectives:
Interpret and analyze domestic and international macroeconomic data.
Apply macroeconomic models to explain economic issues and outcomes.
Analyze the effects of macroeconomic policies.
Part 2 - Local Course Objectives:
Identify and demonstrate a knowledge of the nature and scope of economics, including the definition of "scarcity" and its consequences.
Interpret and develop economic graphs, including production possibilities, supply shifters and demand shifters as they relate to concepts of efficiency and equilibrium in the market economy.
Identify and apply the necessary elements of a "market system" and compare them to other systems of economic organization, referencing ideas as diverse as Frederick Von Hayek and Joseph Stiglitz.
Analyze and interpret various economic models, such as production possibilities frontiers, supply and demand, aggregate supply (AS) and aggregate demand (AD).

Demonstrate and apply concept of equilibrium level of real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) by applying aggregate supply/demand concepts and evaluate the various policies that can be applied to achieve desirable equilibrium levels, including fiscal policy evaluation in the traditional Keynesian-cross, graphical expenditure model (complete with government spending, tax and international trade components).
Calculate and measure macroeconomic variables such as Gross Domestic Product (GDP), real GDP, national income, unemployment, and inflation.
Distinguish various causes of unemployment and inflation, and predict the probable winners and losers from unemployment and inflation.
Illustrate and explain the components of the money supply, how banks create money, and how the Federal Reserve controls the money-creating powers of banks.

Identify and describe the tools of "fiscal policy" and "monetary policy" and apply them to various economic situations such as unemployment and inflation to evaluate policy effectiveness in terms of reaching the (sometimes conflicting) goals of macroeconomic management of the economy.

Recognize and predict the likely short-run and long-run consequences (such as moral hazard) of a given fiscal and/or monetary policy action and assess the significance of new institutional tools of macroeconomic coordination such as the Term Auction Facility and the Asset-Backed Securities Loan Facility.

Demonstrate a knowledge of the nature and scope of international trade (gains from trade and comparative advantage) and international finance as these areas apply to the analysis all of the topics above.
Perform comparative analysis of the relative merits of monetary and fiscal policies, assessing these macroeconomic interventions with IS-LM graphical analysis.
Analyze and evaluate the macroeconomic impact of asymmetric information, moral hazard and adverse selection in specific market sectors such as health care, insurance and financial markets.

objectives: Observe and reflect on lived religious practice
Connect your experience to key course concepts and theories
Practice cross-cultural understanding and respectful engagement
Guidelines:
Choose a Religious Tradition New to You
You may not attend a service from your own religious upbringing or belief system.
Choose a tradition covered in class that you have little or no prior personal exposure to.
Visit a Religious Site or Service
Options include temples, mosques, gurdwaras, churches (from different denominations), synagogues, meditation centers, etc.
If in-person is not possible, you may attend a live-streamed service or virtual tour with permission from your instructor.
Before the Visit
Do basic research: What is the name of the religion? What are common practices and beliefs?
Reach out respectfully, if needed, to ask about dress code, customs, and visitor expectations.
During the Visit
Be respectful and attentive. Take mental notes (or discreet notes if allowed) on what you see, hear, and feel.
Observe rituals, music, symbols, architecture, interactions, and overall atmosphere.
Write Your Reflection Report
Your report must include:
Introduction: Briefly state the tradition you visited, the name and location of the site, and why you chose it.
Descriptive Summary: Describe what you observed, including physical setting, rituals, participation, and sensory details.
Thematic Analysis: Use at least two concepts or theories of religion from the course (e.g., myth, ritual, Durkheim, Eliade, etc.) to interpret your experience.
Personal Reflection: What surprised you? What challenged your assumptions? What questions did it raise?
Conclusion: Reflect on the value of engaging religious diversity through lived experience.
Formatting:
Typed, double-spaced, 12-pt font, APA or MLA format
Include any relevant photos, programs, or materials (optional, not required)

rows.title: Religion in America
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
rows.lead: Upon successful completion of this course, students should be able to:
outcomes: Read and critically evaluate primary sources related to religion in America.
Respond critically, analytically, and/or synthetically to issues dealing with religion in America.
Relate the concepts and issues arising in religion in America to contemporary experience.
objectives: Create and articulate a historical, cultural, and/or intellectual matrix within which the concerns and the questions regarding religion in America can be placed.

Read and critically evaluate selected primary sources from religious in America, including but not limited to sacred texts, dialogues, aphorisms, essays, sermons, theological treatises, credal formulae, slave narratives, novels, short stories, and non-textual primary sources such as music and visual art forms, with inclusion of suppressed and/or ignored voices from religion in America.

Respond critically, analytically, and/or synthetically in writing to issues arising in religions in America, including but not limited to the religion and the First Amendment, the historical development of religious traditions in America, the influence of Eastern religions on American religion, and the development of home-grown, syncretistic traditions.
Apply the ideas and concepts arising in the expressions of religion in America to contemporary experience in its social, institutional, psychological, and/or political manifestations.

rows.title: Literature and Religion of the Bible
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Develop an ability to discuss biblical topics and themes.
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the Jewish Bible, its literature, history and religion.
Demonstrate knowledge and understanding of the Christian Bible, its literature, history and religion.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Introduce and examine the writings which form the basis for moral and religious thinking among Jewish and Christian religious traditions.
Help students develop an understanding of, and tolerance for, cultural and religious differences.
Provide a setting where students use critical thinking in examining the Bible as a major literary source that has historically provided the moral and religious background for the Western world.
Develop a historically based appreciation for the literary styles and thoughts of the authors of the books of the Bible.
Introduce students to the contributions of biblical scholarship over the centuries.

rows.title: Perinatal and Pediatric Respiratory Care
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
The student will know the three cardinal signs of respiratory distress.
The student will identify Laplace’ Law.
The student will know when immature surfactant first appears.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Describe the embryologic development of the cardiopulmonary system
Describe the embryology of the morula, blastocyst, blastoderm, and trophoblast.
Identify the three germ layers and the body structures that evolve from each.
Identify the five periods of embryonic lung growth and describe the features of each period.
Define surface tension and describe the following: (a) How it is developed, (b) Laplace's law, (c) Application to alveolar mechanics

With regard to surfactant, describe the following: (a) function and purpose, (b) the approximate gestational age at which immature and mature surfactant appear, (c) and components and methods to detect its presence
Regarding fetal lung fluid, describe the following: (a)composition, (b) function, (c) the hazards of lung fluid retention
Describe the embryologic development of the heart including: (a) development of the cardiac chambers (b) the formation of major vessels and cardiac valves

With regard to fetal circulation, describe and explain: (a) The cause of pressure differences between the right and left heart (b) the low of blood from the placenta, throught the body and back to the placenta (c) Each shunt that is encountered
Describe the location and function of the baroreceptors and chemoreceptors.
Describe the development of the placenta and umbilical cord and identify the major anatomical structures of each.
Explain the function of amniotic fluid and define the following: (a) Polyhydramnios (b) Oligohydramnios
Describe the assessment of fetal growth and development
Describe at least three ways ultrasonography is used to assess fetal age.

Define amniocentesis and describe the role of each of the following: (1) L/S ratio (b) determination of alpha-fetoprotein (c) bilirubin level (d) creatinine level (e) identification of meconium staining (f) cytologic examination of cells
Describe three different methods of measuring fetal heart rate.
Describe the cause and/or characteristics of the following: (a) baseline heart rate (b) Bradycardia (c) tachycardia (d) beat-to-beat variability (e)cardiac accelerations (f) cardiac decelerations
Explain how fetal scalp pH is used to assess fetal asphyxia.
List and describe the five methods used to estimate the date of delivery.
Compare and contrast the contraction stress test to the non-stress test. Describe how each test is performed, and their advantages and disadvantages.
Describe the use of vibro acoustic stimulation, fetal movements, and amniotic fluid volume as methods of assessing fetal well-being.
Describe the six tests used in the biophysical profile, and how each is scored.
Explain the implications of meconium-stained amniotic fluid in assessing fetal status.
Describe chorionic villus sampling, cordocentesis, and magnetic resonance imaging in assessing fetal status.
Compare and contrast material estriol determination and human placental lactogen levels as to their roles in determining fetal status.
Identify and list at least five factors that indicate a high-risk pregnancy.
List the five events that make up the birth process.
Compare and contrast cervical dilatation and effacement.
Identify the most common presentation.
Define station and how it is expressed.
Describe the sequence of events that lead to the descent and delivery of the fetus.
Define tocolysis and describe the various methods used to achieve tocolysis.
Define dystocia and describe the three etiologic factors that cause it.

Describe each of the following: (a) complete breech (b) incomplete or footling breech (c) Frank breech (d) face presentation (e) transferse lie (f) prolapse of umbilical cord and occult cord compression
Identify and describe the three types of placenta previa.
Describe the three categories of abruptio placentae.
List the indications for a cesarean birth.
Explain why multiple gestations create high-risk pregnancies.
List factors that are responsible for the first breath.
Describe the importance of overcoming surface forces in adapting to extrauterine life.
Identify and describe factors that cause the change from fetal to adult circulation.
List the four factors that can lead to fetal asphyxia.
Compare and contrast primary to secondary apnea. Describe the cardiovascular events that occur during periods of intrauterine asphyxia.
Discuss the effects of asphyxia on the lungs.
List and describe the three factors that provide proper preparation for resuscitation.
Describe the ABCs of resuscitation. Include a description of the "continuing circle" of resuscitation.
Assign an appropriate Apgar score when provided with patient data.
Describe and discuss each step in recuscitation.

Describe each of the following skills as it relates to neonatal recuscitation:(a) thermoregulation (b) suctioning (c) positioning (d) tactile stimulation (e) evaluation of respirations (f) evaluation of heart rate (g) positive pressure ventilation (h) chest compressions (i) intubation (j) delivery of medications
List the drugs used during resuscitation. Include correct concentrations used, dosages, and routes of administration.
Describe the procedure for obtaining arterial blood from the umbilical stump.
Discuss the indications, procedure for placement, and complications of an umbilical artery catheter (UAC).
Describe the sources of fetal and neonatal glucose.
List the serum glucose values that indicate hypoglycemia. Include a description of the clinical signs.
List and describe the cause of hypoglycemia, techniques used to measure glucose, and the treatment for hypoglycemia.
Perform assessment of the Neonatal and Pediatric Patient
State at least ten anatomic and physiologic differences between the infant and the adult.
Given a patient's obstetrical history (PARA), identify the following: previous pregnancies, miscarriages; premature births; and living children.
Identify the physical and neurologic signs examined in the Dubowitz and the Ballard Gestational Age Assessments.
Compare and contrast the Dubowitz and Ballard gestational age assessments.
Describe seven physical signs that are used to determine gestational age. Relate findings of each to varying gestational ages.
List five purposes of the neonatal physical examination.

Describe each of the following as it pertains to the physical examination. Include a description of the unique aspects of each examination. (a) quiet examination (b) hands-on examination (c) neurologic examination
Identify and state the twelve questions that should be evaluated during the history-taking portion of the pediatric examination.
List the three goals to be achieved when examining the pediatric pulmonary system. Include a description of how each goal is assessed.
List the four indications for performing pulmonary function tests on neonates and pediatric patients
Describe the two methods used to measure compliance and resistance, and the two methods used to measure expiratory flows in the neonatal patient
Describe the two methods used to measure compliance and resistance, and the two methods used to measure expiratory flows in the neonatal patient.
Describe the use of helium dilution, nitrogen washout, and body plethysmography in assessing lung volumes
When shown a volume-pressure loop, determine whether it is normal, or demonstrates abnormal compliance or resistance.
Describe the special requirements needed when assessing pulmonary function on the pediatric patient
List the indications for airway clearance

Describe each of the following airway clearance techniques: (a) positive expiratory pressure (b) forced exhalation technique (c) autogenic drainage (d) high-frequency chest compression (e) flutter valve therapy
Describe the procedure for performing chest physiotherapy (CPT) including: (a) auscultation (b) postural drainage (c) percussion (d) vibration (e) removal of secretions
Discuss the following as they apply to aerosol delivery: (a) particle amount (b) particle size (c) particle characteristics (d) airway anatomy (e) ventilatory pattern
Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of each of the following: (a) small volume nebulizer (b) metered dose inhaler (c) dry powder inhaler
List the indications for aerosolized drug therapy
Describe the equipment used to deliver aerozolized medications. Compare and contrast updraft nebulizers to mainstream nebulizers
Discuss the procedure for placement of a medication nebulizer inline to a ventilator circuit
List and describe the hazards of aerosolized medications
Explain the techniques used to prevent ventilator malfunction when aerosolizing ribavirin into a ventilator circuit
Describe the indications for and hazards of suctioning and the equipment used.
Discuss the indications for and hazards of oxygen therapy
Describe, for each of the following, its role in oxygen delivery: (a) oxygen blenders and flowmeters (b) oxygen analyzers
Compare and contrast bubble and wick humidifiers

Describe the indications, hazards, and approximate FIO2 for each of the following: (a) oxygen hood (b) oxygen cannula (c) simple oxygen mask (d) nonrebreating mask (e) venturi mask (f) tent (g) incubator (h) resuscitation bags
Discuss the physiology of thermoregulation, including a description of the thermoneutral zone and nonshivering thermogenesis
Define the internal thermal gradient (ITG) and describe the reasons why a preemie has a decreased ability to maintain its ITG

Describe each of the following as it relates to the external thermal gradient. Include examples for each type of heat loss and a description of how each method of heat loss may be prevented or reduced in the nursery (a) radiant (b) conductive (c) convective (d) evaporative

rows.title: Advanced Respiratory Care Clinical Application I
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
The student will demonstrate how to extubate a patient using proper procedure and universal precaution.
The student will demonstrate how to secure a nasal or oral ET tube on a patient.
The student will demonstrate how to perform a minimum leak technique or a minimal occluding volume for cuff inflation on intubated or trached patient.

The student will demonstrate how to change a ventilator circuit when indicated, maintaining clean technique and assuring minimal interruption of ventilation on a patient in an acute care or alternate care site.
The student will demonstrate how to draw arterial blood sample via needle and syringe from a patient, using proper procedure and universal precautions.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:

In both a simulated patient-care environment and the hospital setting, satisfactorily demonstrate mastery of 50% of the advanced-level performance skills listed in the Second-Year Clinical Syllabus (attached).
Assess patients and recommend therapy.

Evaluate pertinent historical and physiologic data to include: Lab statistice and monitoring data

rows.title: Medical Ethics and Patient Advocacy
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Analyze, compare, and evaluate a variety of moral theories (such as Utilitarianism, Kantianism, Natural Law, or Human Rights theory) that are relevant to problems in medical ethics.

Apply theories in normative ethics to specific problems or controversies in medical ethics, e.g., experimentation, informed consent, allocation of resources, use of technologies, abortion, medically assisted dying, etc.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Interpret primary and/or secondary sources in moral theory (e.g., Utilitarianism, Kantianism, etc.) as a philosophical background to medical ethics.
Compare and contrast a variety of theoretical approaches to moral reasoning in relation to issues in medical ethics.

Explore a variety of moral concerns that arise in medical contexts (e.g., allocation of medical resources, uses of medical technology, responsibilities of medical professionals, etc.) by reading academic articles on these topics.
Apply theoretical approaches to a variety of specific contemporary problems in medical and bio-ethics (e.g., euthanasia, abortion, genetic screening, medical experimentation, etc.)
Investigate prominent Case Studies in the area of medical ethics, e.g., Roe v. Wade (1973), Oregon's Death With Dignity Act (1994), Molly and Adam Nash (2000), Terri Schiavo (2005), etc.
Identify the relevant factual information and ethical dimensions of various problems and controversies in medical ethics.
Examine controversial issues in medical ethics in a manner that is charitable and fair to those having different or opposing perspectives.
Evaluate an argument in medical ethics using rigorous methods of critical thinking.
Think critically about issues in medical ethics and support a particular position with evidence and reasons.
Apply philosophical ideas, theories, and methods to defend a position on a topic in medical ethics with a clear and well-developed argument.

objectives: Part 1 - Common Course Numbering Objectives:

Identify appropriate statistical techniques and use technology-based statistical analysis to describe, interpret, and communicate results.

Part 2 - Local Course Objectives:
Recognize the proper use of statistics and distinguish them from the abuse of statistics.

Construct and interpret confidence intervals.

Run various tests of hypotheses on various types of sample statistics, while appropriately using the Central Limit Theorem.

Use effective communication and collaborative skills with the interprofessional health care team to deliver evidence-based patient-centered care.
Incorporate effective communication techniques to foster positive professional working relationships.
Access data and documents using the nursing process via electronic health record, abiding by all ethical and legal standards.
Demonstrate the use of information technology systems, at a foundational level, to prevent the risk of errors and improve clinical outcomes in the delivery of safe patient care.
Competently use patient care technologies, information systems, d. and communication devices that support safe nursing care.
Incorporate quality improvement principles to identify potential problems that may interfere with the delivery of safe patient care.
Participate in guided self-reflection activities to identify professional learning needs.
Perform ongoing evaluation of expected outcomes and interventions and participate in the revision of the individualized plan of care as needed.
Collect data to assist the registered nurse in problem identification, goal attainment, and the selection of interventions based on the patient’s health care needs.
Demonstrate clinical reasoning and judgment skills when providing quality, safe patient-centered care
Demonstrate computer literacy, including the ability to use desktop applications and mobile technology to promote communication and support decision-making.

rows.title: Essential Customer Service
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify essential customer needs and demands.
Communicate effectively, both verbally and nonverbally.
Identify e-customer needs and meet their demands
Interact effectively face-to-face, by telephone and by e-mail
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Display courtesy and respect by making a great first impression, speaking and acting appropriately, maintaining a positive attitude, and acting ethically.
Communicate well by saying what you mean to say, projecting proper body language, asking and answering questions correctly, and listening carefully.
Build strong relationships by establishing a rapport, interacting positively with customers, identifying needs, and finding the best solution.
Handle customers skillfully in fact-to-face, telephone, Web site, and self-service settings.
Satisfy customers who are upset or difficult.

rows.title: Essential Workplace Computer Skills
rows.heading: Student Learning Outcomes
outcomes: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Identify the major categories/types and components of modern computers.
Create, format, modify, and save a document using word processing software.
Create a spreadsheet file, enter data into worksheets, and perform calculations on the data using spreadsheet software.
Demonstrate use of tools and techniques for navigating and searching internet resources
Use common computer communication applications to create and manage contacts, and schedule and update meetings and appointments.
objectives: Upon satisfactory completion of the course, students will be able to:
Differentiate between different types of computers.
Identify basic personal computing hardware.
Use system software to perform basic computer navigation, file management, and maintenance tasks.
Identify and efficiently use keyboards, pointing devices and touchscreens.
Identify and use peripheral devices, including scanners and printers.
Install and use application software to enhance productivity.
Identify, select, and use a word processing application and embedded features such as spell check, thesaurus, editing and formatting tools.
Identify, select, and use a spreadsheet processing and embedded features such as simple functions, cell editing and sheet formatting.
Identify and use data storage media located on computers, usb devices, and the cloud.
Connect to and use the Internet.
Identify and utilize workplace relevant Internet research techniques.
Enhance personal management and communication through effective use of email, video conferencing, chat, online calendars and task managers, and contact directories.
